dedupe_keys.name: climate change allowances in network rail drainage standards across the british railway network

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes how Network Rail, the infrastructure manager for the railway in Great Britain, added climate change allowances to its drainage standards under its Weather Resilience and Climate Change Adaptation (WRCCA) strategy. Water drives scour of bridges and embankments and softening of the track support system, flooding was the main weather cause of delays in 2012 to 2017, and weather costs £50 to £100 million a year in delays and cancellations alone. The standards raise design flows and capacity of new and refurbished drainage in line with Environment Agency flood allowances and UKCP18 projections, and route WRCCA plans turn them into local works, such as flood remediation at Dalmarnock, Drem and Penmanshiel in Scotland and a 20 percent extra drainage capacity with a £40 million drainage programme on the South East route in Control Period 6 (2019 to 2024). Implementation started in 2011, with a 60-year design life for drainage. The page, first published in 2016 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML with a link to Network Rail's adaptation pages. Caveats: the page reports plans for only 3 of 8 routes for CP6, gives no network-wide cost, and upgrading existing drainage depends on available resources. The case illustrates climate adaptation of design standards and resilience of rail assets to flooding; related records are the French transport standards review, the ÖBB Alpine hazards case study and ERA RINF.
name: Climate change allowances in Network Rail drainage standards across the British railway network
outcomes: Drainage standards now include climate change allowances; the South East route adds 20% drainage design capacity and plans £40 million of drainage improvements in CP6, and several Scottish flood sites were remediated in CP5.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study from Network Rail
resources_used: Environment Agency flood risk climate change allowances
